records.text: The fork lands. A single attacker now has several victims, and usually only one of them gets away. Notebook rule: study the square it came from.
There is a forking square in the other side's reach. One enemy piece can land where it hits several targets together. I want every enemy landing square checked first.
A fork went begging. Another move sent one piece after several targets together. From today, forks belong in the scan before every move.
The pin holds. Stepping off that line would expose the king behind, so the piece in front is frozen there. Pile more pressure onto a frozen piece.
Pinning chances go to the other side here. One piece would be stuck on the line to its own king, unable to step off. Notebook rule: keep pieces off the lines that lead to the king.
A pin was waiting. With another move, a piece would have been stuck in front of its king. I want every line through the king examined.
The skewer bites. The front piece is attacked, and when it steps off the line, the piece behind it is next. Lines like this pay out.
Two pieces sharing one line is an invitation, and this lets the other side skewer them. Notebook rule: never stack valuable pieces where one attack hits both.
A skewer stayed in the box. Another move attacked the front piece with the back one waiting behind. From today, look past every target.
Guard eliminated. Whatever it was protecting may now be loose. Follow up on its old duties straight away.
A guard under threat. The other side can now capture a defender, and what it protects would lose its cover. Notebook rule: know which defenders carry the load.
The guard should have gone. Another move captured the defender and left its duties uncovered. Strike the guard first, then what it guards.
The back rank gives way. The king's own pieces fence it in, and it has nowhere to run. That pattern is worth hunting every game.
The back rank is brittle. The king is walled in by its own pieces, and this gives the other side a mating idea along the last rank. Give the king air before it is needed.
The back rank was open for business. The king had no exit square, and a back-rank mating idea was there to use. Test the last rank whenever a king is boxed in.
The pawn is on its way. Its goal is the last rank and a new piece. I want the promotion race counted for both sides.
Keep that pawn in sight. One of the other side's pawns now has an open road to promotion. Every passed pawn gets a count, whoever owns it.
The pawn should have marched. A stronger move pushed it toward promotion, and this one holds it back. Advanced pawns get counted every single turn.
The hidden attacker appears. One piece steps aside, and the piece behind takes aim down the line it uncovered. Make the moving piece threaten something too.
A hidden attacker is ready. This lets one enemy piece step aside and open a line for the piece behind it. Notebook rule: watch what stands behind their pieces.
A discovered attack was ready. Another move opened a line for a piece waiting behind. Look at what stands behind every piece on the board.
Double duty. This creates two threats at the same time, and the reply can usually answer just one. That is the pressure to aim for.
Too much to answer. This lets the other side threaten two things at once. Check the replies that carry more than one threat.
A double attack was waiting. A stronger move created two threats together, and this one creates neither. Search for the move that does two jobs.
The defender is dragged away. A deflection drags it off duty, leaving its square unwatched. Learn what each defender is tied down by.
An overloaded defender. This lets the other side lure it away from its duty. Notebook rule: never give one defender two jobs.
The deflection was on. A different move would have pulled a defender away from its post. When a defender has two duties, hit one of them.
Free material, collected. Nothing protected that piece, so no recapture follows. Take what is free, then look further.
Free material stayed on the board. Nothing guarded that piece, and it was left alone. Count every loose piece before a quiet move.
A piece left hanging. Nothing defends it now, and the other side can simply take it. Notebook rule: count defenders before letting go of the move.
Catch this detail. This move pulls away the one real defender, and the piece it was guarding is now there for the taking. Before any defender moves, name its duty.
The threat had to come first. The opponent's last move went after a piece, this move paid it no attention, and now that piece can be captured. I want every turn to start with their threat.
The arithmetic failed. This capture runs into a recapture that collects more than it gave up. Finish the count, recapture included, before starting a trade.
Another piece joins the fight. A knight or bishop leaves home for active duty. Keep counting how many are still at home.
Development was on offer. Another move would have brought out a minor piece. Compare it with what the game saw.
A clear run down the file for the rook. No pawns of either color stand on that file, so the rook owns its length. That is where rooks do their best work.
A highway for a rook was one move away. Another move put a rook on a file without pawns. Hunt for those files when placing rooks.
A file with a target. It is semi-open for the rook, with none of its own pawns there and at least one enemy pawn to press. Aim the rook at that pawn.
A semi-open file was within reach. Another move gave a rook a file free of its own pawns and holding at least one enemy pawn. Set that placement against this one.
A passed pawn is born. No enemy pawn blocks or guards its path, on its file or the neighboring ones. Advance it when it is safe.
A passed pawn was available. Another move would have given a pawn a clear road, with no enemy pawn able to block or capture it on the way. Learn which pawn breaks make passers.
The passer moves up. It stands one square nearer promotion now. Keep it protected on the way.
The passer could have moved. Another move pushed it one square nearer promotion. Keep a passed pawn rolling whenever it is safe.
A pawn is cut off. Neither neighboring file has a friendly pawn to support it. Plan around that weakness, whichever side owns it.
Another move would have cut a pawn off from its neighbors, with no friendly pawn on the files beside it. Set that structure beside this one.
Cover restored. The piece that stood without protection has a defender again. Loose pieces get checked every move.
Cover was on offer. Another move gave an unprotected piece a defender. Compare which pieces each move leaves loose.
A piece stands alone. No defender covers it. That is a weakness to watch, not a lost piece.
Another move would have stripped a piece of its defenders. On its own that loses nothing, but note it.
The king gets air. A new legal square opens up for it. Make room like that before trouble arrives.
Air for the king was one move away. Another move opened a new legal square for it. Mating a king with room takes more work.
The king is tucked away. Castling moved king and rook in a single turn, with the rook settling next to the king. Safety first, then the real work.
Castling was on the table. King and rook could have moved together in one turn. Compare the king's safety in both lines.
No more bishop pair. One bishop has been captured, so that side covers only one square color with bishops. Count that in every trade.
Another move took a bishop, and with it the other side's pair. Know what each trade does to the bishops.
Doubled pawns. Two pawns of the same color stand on one file, and they cannot defend each other. Write that structure down.
Another move would have doubled pawns on a single file. Compare what each structure costs.
This decides the game. After this move, checkmate is forced. Forcing replies get looked at before anything else, every move.
Mate was there to be had. Checkmate was forced, and this move walks away from it. When a king is short of squares, test every check.
The sacrifice holds. The material is there to take, and the idea survives anyway in the line we checked. Learn the line that follows the capture.
A narrow path. Every other checked move failed, and this one kept the game going. Put that defense on repeat in practice.
A thin margin was required. No other checked move held on to the advantage. Remember how thin that path was.
Material is falling. A capture is ready on the very next move. Look at what hangs after every move.
Expect the forcing answer. The strongest reply here gives check, so the king must be handled first. Checks go into every calculation.
There was a better move. The engine prefers another choice in this position. Study both until the difference is clear.
That has a price. Value slips away compared with the engine's top choice. Put the stronger move beside this one and study both.
Up to standard. A strong move, and very little value given up.

That was your call, and a good one. Few would play it, the human-move model estimates, and the engine still rates it strong. Good chess sometimes looks unusual.
Hard, but it was there. Exactly one checked move kept the position playable, a difficult one by the human-move model's reading. That defense becomes your practice position.

Sound instinct. This is the move the human-move model predicted, and the engine ranks it first. Trust judgment like that.
Sound instinct. This was the human-move model's expected move, and the engine rates it strong, close to its top choice. Keep building on it.

A proper repair. The piece that was hanging loose earlier has protection once more. Keep an eye on it.

Well executed. Mate, and the win belongs to you.
